newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Cyprus sceptical of British proposal.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus sceptical of British proposal.

text.p: A British proposal for ending the stalemate between Greeks and Turks on divided Cyprus did not go far enough to justify direct talks between the rival communities, Cyprus said on Tuesday.

"This does not constitute common ground," Cypriot government spokesman Yiannakis Cassoulides told reporters on Tuesday when asked to comment on a 10-point proposal announced on Monday by British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind.

Rifkind, who visited the island to propel rival Greek and Turkish Cypriot sides towards peace talks, presented the proposals at a news conference before his departure. He said they offered the best basis for progress.

"Much work is needed for a ray of hope of an agreement on the five basic issues which constitute the Cyprus problem," Cassoulides said, referring to issues relating to sovereignty, territory, security, guarantees and the settlement of persons displaced after Turkey invaded in 1974 in response to a coup engineered by the military junta in Greece.
Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash, who heads a breakaway state in northern Cyprus recognised only by Ankara, has called for talks with Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides.

The Greek Cypriot side, internationally recognised as the government of Cyprus, will consent to face-to-face talks with the Turkish Cypriots only when common ground is found on the basic issues which could ensure a successful dialogue.

In his 10-point proposal Rifkind said the boundaries of a future federation of Cyprus should not follow the present ceasefire line. A federal state should be accorded international guarantees, and he called on both sides to take steps to encourage mutual confidence as the parties slowly made peace.
The proposals, which did not contain any new element relating to the Cyprus problem, were criticised by Greek Cypriot political parties on Tuesday for "glaring discrepancies".

Communist Akel, the island's second largest and main opposition party, said Rifkind's failure to refer to a federal Cyprus with one sovereignty and citizenship -- included in all U.N. resolutions on Cyprus -- was a cause for concern.
"This omission is very serious and causes concern and questions," Akel said.
Rifkind spoke only of one "international personality" in his proposals.
The United Nations have been trying to reunite the island as a bicommunal bi-zonal federation for decades without success.
Tension has increased perceptibly on the island in the past six months after the deaths of four people in ceasefire line incidents as both sides continue to build up their defences.

Some 35,000 Turkish troops are stationed in northern Cyprus. The 11,500-strong Greek Cypriot national guard is weaker both in military hardware and personnel but is engaged in a comprehensive programme to upgrade its defences.
Rifkind described the level of militarisation as "absurdly high and dangerously high".

Reports that Russia plans to sell Cyprus a surface-to-air missile system are expected to dominate talks that Turkey's Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller is due to have with the Russian government this week.
The Greek Cypriots say the buildup is purely for defensive purposes.
"If the Turkish occupation forces were here with slingshots and stones our equipment would be different," Cassoulides said.
